chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
title: The 1942 six-piece band at the Crystal Caverns; John Hammond wants more blues
summary: With Osie Johnson, Phil Phillips, Charlie Rouse, Tommy Potter and Harry Curtis he plays small-band arrangements, and John Hammond complains they play too little blues.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Anyway, Osie was one of those people who was just an excellent musician. He worked with Earl Hines' band... Well, after our band, we had this... I don't want to get ahead of myself here. After the guys began to go into the Army, Osie Johnson, Leonard Phillips and a fellow named Harry Curtis, an alto player (Leonard Phillips, the trumpet player, Osie Johnson, the drummer), Tommy Potter (bass), and a young tenor saxophone player who was 18 then, and he was also at Armstrong High School, and his name was Charlie Rouse -- we formed a band, a six-piece band. We worked at this famous club, as far as Washington goes, called the Crystal Caverns. It's the one I was telling you about where Jimmy Mundy wrote this tune called "Cavernism." Well, we worked there, and this was in 1942. It was during the war...

We had a very good little band, and Osie and I wrote some six-piece arrangements that all the musicians that came from around the country, and came to the Howard Theatre, and they would come down and hear us, and admire us for sounding like a big band. But at this time, Osie and I were experimenting with all kinds of arrangements. Sometimes on ballads behind

singers or something, we would write things with the tenor saxophone, the alto and the trumpet, and maybe have a bass (?) or a fourth part to be like a horn, and we'd stretch the harmonies out. It was a very nice little band. And people came down there...

Even John Hammond came down, who was then responsible for the Basie band, I understand... The thing that John Hammond didn't like about our band was that we didn't play enough Blues, you know. And at that particular time, we were experimenting with all kinds of chords and harmonies, and we weren't that much into the Blues as we should have been. We didn't realize just what Blues really meant. We played some Blues and stuff like that, but we were more or less into experimenting and arranging things more intricate with rhythms, and we were listening to people like Jimmy Lunceford and Duke Ellington, Earl Hines. We actually played more Blues-type things when we had the big band, because we played more Basie-type things. But in this little band, we were experimenting with all kinds of voicings and stuff.
